title: Bio
text: Lancelot Da Costa is a postdoctoral researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems in Tübingen, working with Bernhard Schölkopf. He received his PhD in Mathematics from Imperial College London, advised by Grigorios Pavliotis and Karl Friston, and his thesis won the Best Maths PhD Thesis Prize. He previously worked at VERSES with Karl Friston and interned at MILA with Yoshua Bengio, after studying mathematics and neuroscience at EPFL, Cambridge and UCL. His work formalized the free-energy principle, an influential theory of brain function, and he now develops AI that learns like we do, through active world modeling. He leads ATOM, a focused research community working on these questions.

title: Research
text:
What I cannot create, I do not understand. (Richard Feynman)
I work on machines that learn like we do: by actively exploring and building models of the world, an approach I call active world modeling.
A toddler putting a new object in their mouth is running an experiment: testing what it is made of and how it behaves, and revising their model of it. State-of-the-art AI mostly learns differently, by passively absorbing vast amounts of data.
Learning in nature seems to follow general principles, on which developmental psychology, cognitive science, neuroscience and physics increasingly converge. My research bet is that building on these principles can give us AI that learns autonomously, continually and open-endedly from far less data and compute, generalizes and adapts when the world changes, and is aligned, safer and more robust.

title: Research
text:
Active world modeling
Active world modeling agents learn how their world works, including what kind of model best describes it, while acting to gain information and achieve goals safely. Making this work raises mathematical, statistical and engineering challenges. We are working on three interlinked questions:

Universal world modeling. Which models can describe anything from physical to social interactions, while still letting an agent learn as efficiently as possible? (Da Costa, 2024; Da Costa et al., 2026)
Model discovery. How can an agent infer which models best explain its experience, from a handful of observations to vast amounts of data? (Da Costa et al., 2025; Six, Panse, Fajeau, Da Costa et al., 2026)
Active learning. How should an agent act to improve its understanding of the world while pursuing its goals safely? (see Rainforth et al., 2023 for a review)

title: Research
text:
Where this comes from
My work has developed three interlocking strands. First, I formalized principles of biological intelligence, such as the free-energy principle, through Bayesian mechanics: a mathematical account of how systems that persist in a changing environment can be described as inferring the world around them (Da Costa et al., 2021; Friston, Da Costa et al., 2023). Second, I helped formalize active inference, the theory of agents that follows from these principles: agents perceive and learn by approximate Bayesian inference, and plan by balancing expected utility with information gain (Da Costa et al., 2020; Barp, Da Costa, França et al., 2022). Similar principles, developed independently in cognitive science, have produced agents that reach human-level sample efficiency in simple video games (Tsividis et al., 2021).
These agents, however, rely on world models whose structure is designed by hand, which limits them to simple environments. Active world modeling, my current focus, is the main missing ingredient for scaling this approach: agents that learn not only the contents of their world models but also their structure (Da Costa et al., 2025).

title: Research

I lead ATOM Research, a focused research community developing active world modeling and scaling it toward an agent foundation model: agents that learn autonomously and continually, are sample- and compute-efficient, generalize and adapt when the world changes, and are aligned, safe and robust.

title: Hi, I’m Lance!
text:
I am a mathematician working toward understanding and building intelligence. My work formalized an influential theory of brain function, and I now use these ideas to develop AI that learns like we do: by actively exploring and building models of the world, an approach I call active world modeling.
Currently I work as a postdoc at the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems with Bernhard Schölkopf, and I lead ATOM, a focused research community of students and researchers working on these questions. Previously, I worked at VERSES with Karl Friston and interned at MILA with Yoshua Bengio.
I have authored over 50 papers across artificial intelligence, mathematics, physics and neuroscience, and received the Best Maths PhD Thesis Prize from Imperial College London in 2025, a Best Paper award from Entropy, and excellence awards from the American Physical Society, G-Research, UK’s EPSRC, Luxembourg’s National Research Fund, Imperial College London, and others.

title: Current Thoughts on Causal Representation Learning vs Deep Generative Modeling and What Might Be Next
text: A research note. I am trying to pin down how causal representation learning (CRL) actually differs from deep generative modeling, and find that they are much more similar than they seem. I am writing this partly to preserve the confusion rather than to resolve it, and partly to sketch some thoughts as to what may come next. Note that I am not an expert in CRL and may be missing many important points.

title: Current Thoughts on Causal Representation Learning vs Deep Generative Modeling and What Might Be Next
section: Deep generative modeling vs Causal Representation Learning
text:
Deep generative modeling vs Causal Representation Learning
Both deep generative modeling and CRL train models on data by maximizing likelihood. That much seems uncontroversial.
In ordinary deep learning we usually do conditional maximum likelihood: we map inputs to outputs and maximize \(\log p_\theta(y \mid x)\). In deep generative modeling we maximize the likelihood of the data itself, \(\log p_\theta(x)\), often with latent variables and a variational bound (Kingma and Welling 2014). In CRL, as I understand it, the stated goal is to identify a generative causal model — the right variables, the right graph — and we typically do this, again, by maximizing likelihood (Schölkopf et al. 2021).
So where is the difference? The cleanest distinction I can find is the data: CRL usually assumes access to observational and interventional/action data, whereas deep generative modeling usually has only observations. But once I strip away the data difference, fitting a causal generative model by maximum likelihood starts to look like we are solving the same statistical problem as deep generative modeling, except perhaps with a different model class, different regularizers, and different optimization dynamics.
CRL also emphasizes that the variables and connections should be meaningful, and that the graph should be sparse. But “meaningful” feels close to “interpretable,” and interpretability usually requires small models. And sparsity is a complexity prior. So now the contrast reads: deep learning fits the data and (somehow) controls complexity, and CRL fits the data and (explicitly) controls complexity. That is the same goal stated twice.
Here is a move that shrinks down the distinction. If we want to search over causal graphs, a standard and useful relaxation is to let the discrete “connected / not connected” edges become continuous weights, so that gradient descent can do the searching. But the moment we do that, we are back to optimizing a continuous, over-parameterized model by gradient descent — which is just deep learning. Deep nets are over-parameterized and (hopefully) discover useful sub-models through gradient descent, regularization and architecture choices; CRL tries to build the right small model from scratch. But if both relax to continuous optimization, they meet in the middle.

title: Current Thoughts on Causal Representation Learning vs Deep Generative Modeling and What Might Be Next
text:
A possible over-strong consequence
The tempting conclusion: there is no real difference between CRL and deep learning. Both aim at maximum likelihood while minimizing complexity. Deep learning controls complexity implicitly — through regularization and generalization to held-out data (and if natural data has low Kolmogorov complexity, optimizing for generalization should favor simpler solutions (Goldblum et al. 2024)). CRL controls complexity explicitly — through meaningful, sparse structure.
I think this strong version must be too strong, but I want to be careful about why. Let me separate the cases:

If CRL means fitting a neural generative model with latent variables, then yes, it looks like deep generative modeling.
If CRL means recovering the right causal variables and mechanisms under explicit assumptions, then it is a sharper and harder problem — this is the identifiability program, and it is genuinely different.
If CRL means fitting causal models to action-observation data, then it is close to deep generative modeling but with a much richer data stream.

So the real difference, if there is one, lives in two places: identifiability and the action/intervention signal. The rest is, I suspect, the same machine.

The identifiability program, and the ground-truth problem
A lot of CRL is identifiability-based (Locatello et al. 2019; Khemakhem et al. 2020; Ahuja et al. 2022; Lachapelle et al. 2021). The question is: if I fit a causal model by maximum likelihood, do I recover the right causal variables, and under what conditions? That is a real and important question that deep generative modeling rarely even asks.
But here is what nags at me. Identifiability results assume a ground-truth causal structure and ask when it can be recovered. In practice we never have access to that ground truth. The ground truth is the world. We only sample it — through sensors and instruments. Even when we intervene, we do not get to see the causal graph; we see more data. And the assumptions that make identifiability theorems go through are often too strong to hold in practice.
So in the absence of theoretical guarantees, what is left of CRL? It seems to reduce to: fit causal models by maximum likelihood to action-observation data. Which is, once more, very close to deep generative modeling — except for the data.


Actions are not just extra labels
This is the part that’s maybe underrated. The interventional/action data in CRL is not a minor footnote — it is a qualitatively richer signal than passive observation. Actions give us:

this action led to this observation;
this sequence of actions led to this sequence of observations;
perturbations that reveal what is controllable and how mechanisms are wired.

That is temporal ordering plus controllability plus mechanism structure, none of which we get from passive data. So I want to flip the usual framing: the mechanism by which CRL is pursued — maximum likelihood on action-observation data — is strictly more powerful than the mechanism of (passive) deep generative modeling — maximum likelihood on observations alone. In that sense CRL is deep generative modeling pointed at a better data stream.
This is reminiscent of the “child as scientist” view from Gopnik and collaborators (Gopnik et al. 1999): children are active learners who run targeted little experiments on the world. Mixing action and observation seems to be the crucial ingredient, not an optional one.


Is the best model really sparse?
CRL leans on sparsity — meaningful variables, few meaningful connections, small graphs — and there’s a common belief that the physical world is sparse, so our models should be too. Sparsity also buys interpretability.
But there’s a counterpoint I want to keep alive. Perhaps a small number of variables explains most of the variance, while a long tail of weak connections explains the small-order effects (Millidge 2025). If so, the best model isn’t strictly sparse — it has a sparse core plus many small weights. And if we insist on capturing all of it, we drift right back toward deep-learning-style dense models. So sparsity might be a good interpretability prior without being the accuracy-optimal structure.
Research question: is the world — and hence the best world model — truly sparse, or is it a sparse core plus a dense tail of small effects? This is both a physics and a machine learning question.

title: Current Thoughts on Causal Representation Learning vs Deep Generative Modeling and What Might Be Next
text:
What might be next
Suppose we grant the deflationary reading — that, mechanism aside, a lot of this is maximum likelihood on action-observation data. Then: what is the next thing to add for next-generation AI? Having actions and temporal dynamics is the clear first move. But there’s a second, and I think it’s important: uncertainty.

Maximum likelihood is the one-particle base case
Maximum likelihood is just Bayes with a flat prior, collapsed to a point estimate. It’s computationally cheap precisely because it keeps a single particle — the current best guess — and throws away the spread. The one thing it loses, relative to fuller versions of variational Bayes, is uncertainty.
Uncertainty is nice for its own sake, but the reason it might be important is for decision-making. If we can maintain uncertainty — over states, parameters, structure, programs, whole models — then we can choose actions that maximize information gain: actions whose resulting observations tell us as much as possible about the world. That is curiosity, planning, and sample efficiency, all falling out of the same calculus. This is essentially the active-inference / Bayesian-decision picture (Da Costa et al. 2020), and there’s a reasonable degree of belief that brains compute and reduce uncertainty for action selection.
So the program I’d state:

maintain uncertainty over (some of the model’s) states, parameters, structure, programs, or architecture;
use that uncertainty for action selection and curiosity;
fit models not just to observations but to action-observation streams;
choose actions that maximize useful information gain/resolve uncertainty about latents.

The research question is scalability. We want uncertainty placed cheaply enough to support real-time decisions under a manageable compute cost. A difficult research question is how to achieve this — and whether a point estimate plus some lightweight machinery can fake the parts of uncertainty we actually need for planning — or whether we genuinely need to carry a distribution.


Candidate stacks
For where to develop this program, I see two co-evolving stacks:

Program induction (Tsividis et al. 2021)
Probabilistic model inference / Bayesian model discovery of which GFlowNets are an example (Bengio et al. 2021)

While the two stacks are distinct in implementation, they seem to be mathematically equivalent. The axis that actually matters from a mathematical perspective is iterative vs. amortized inference. Iterative inference might be slow but could always be doable, while amortized inference is fast once trained.
On GFlowNets specifically: Question: are GFlowNets an instance of amortized inference? My current understanding is that GFlowNet training is iterative inference/optimization, while sampling from a trained GFlowNet is amortized (Malkin et al. 2022). Another question: how do GFlowNets explore the multiple modes of the posterior?
The question with GFlowNets is whether the training can be made to go fast. It’s going to be very good at getting some very accurate posteriors, but maybe this is at the cost of forever being slow? I wonder how fast is state-of-the-art training of deep nets? If GFlowNet training can be made very fast this would be pretty unbeatable because you would have both an extremely accurate posterior and fast dynamics. If there is a bottleneck, then we should look at faster, less accurate approximations — small numbers of particles, say.
Research question: can inference over structures/programs be made fast enough for real-time decision-making? How fast is state-of-the-art deep net training, and does that suggest GFlowNets could be fast enough? If accurate inference is too slow, should we fall back to small-particle approximations?


A speculative neuroscience aside
Working memory seems to hold only a small number of hypotheses at once. But the Thousand Brains theory suggests the cortex runs an enormous number of models in parallel (Hawkins 2021). A tempting picture: we subconsciously maintain very many models/hypotheses, and consciousness/working memory is an attention operator exposing just a few of them. Flag: Check whether Thousand Brains theory really supports the stronger claim that cortical columns are different hypotheses over the world model, or whether the safer claim is that they are semi-independent sensorimotor models. I’m not sure the strong reading is warranted.
Research questions: How many hypotheses/models do we as humans maintain at once? How do multiple models co-evolve — does it look like variational inference, Stein variational gradient descent, GFlowNet training, particle variational inference, or something else? Do the particles/models evolve independently or together and how?

title: Current Thoughts on Causal Representation Learning vs Deep Generative Modeling and What Might Be Next
text:
Upshot

Stripping away the data and assumptions, and CRL and deep generative modeling are both maximum likelihood with a complexity penalty — but we shouldn’t understate the gap.
Yet the gap is real and lives in two places: identifiability (mostly aspirational in practice, since we never see the ground truth) and the action/intervention/temporal signal (genuinely richer, and the part I’m most convinced matters).
Beyond deep generative modeling with action-observation streams, the next step worth chasing is uncertainty placed scalably enough to drive decision-making — curiosity and information-seeking actions on top of action-observation learning.

The focus, then: probabilistic inference over candidate spaces — programs or probabilistic models with better-than-nothing uncertainty tracking — coupled to decision-making that uses that uncertainty.

title: Limitations of Renormalizing Generative Models as Hierarchical Planning Models
text:
This note assumes familiarity with Renormalizing Generative Models (RGMs) (Zaghw et al. 2026; Pashea and Zaghw 2026), especially the fast structure learning procedure (Friston, Heins, et al. 2025; Friston, Parr, et al. 2025; Zaghw et al. 2026). The aim is not to rederive the construction, but to clarify how the learned hierarchy should and should not be interpreted for planning.
Throughout the note, \(o\) denotes sensory observations, \(s^{(1)}\) denotes first-level hidden states, and \(s^{(2)}\) denotes second-level hidden states. A learned higher-level path label is written as \(u^{(2)}\). A controllable high-level action or option is written as \(\beta^{(2)}\). This distinction is important: a learned path label is not automatically a controllable option.
Fast structure learning constructs a hierarchy of predictive models. It groups lower-level variables, turns observed local pattern classes into higher-level states, learns path-conditioned transitions among those states, and passes state/path summaries upward. Read downward, higher-level states provide empirical priors over lower-level initial states and paths through the learned \(D\) and \(E\) mappings.
This construction supports hierarchical inference and prediction. It does not, by itself, establish a valid hierarchy of controllable actions. The central distinction is that observed coarse transitions are not automatically equivalent to controllable high-level actions. The distinction matters because hierarchical planning requires more than a compressed predictive model. A useful planning abstraction must keep the information needed to choose good actions, and it must separate changes the agent can cause from changes it can only observe.

title: Limitations of Renormalizing Generative Models as Hierarchical Planning Models
text:
Statistical Compression as an Assumption
Fast structure learning builds its state and path labels from the training stream. A higher-level state labels a local pattern that appeared in the data. A higher-level path labels a transition branch that appeared in the data. The learned hierarchy therefore reflects what was observed during structure learning.
Consider a local first-level configuration made of two first-level factors,
\[
s_{\mathrm{loc}}^{(1)}
=
(s_a^{(1)},s_b^{(1)}).
\]
If \(s_a^{(1)}\) has \(K_a\) values and \(s_b^{(1)}\) has \(K_b\) values, the full local configuration space contains \(K_aK_b\) configurations. If all configurations appear in the training data and each configuration receives its own second-level label, then the induced second-level state space satisfies
\[
K^{(2)} = K_aK_b.
\]
In that case, the second-level state is primarily a relabelling of the first-level joint configuration. There is no substantive state-space compression.
If only a subset of configurations appears, then
\[
K^{(2)} < K_aK_b.
\]
This reduction has two possible meanings. In the favourable case, it is genuine compression: the omitted or merged distinctions do not matter for later inference or control. In the weaker case, it is only support restriction: the model has fewer states because it only represents the configurations that occurred in the training stream. Fast structure learning does not, by itself, show which interpretation is correct.
This matters for generalization. If a new first-level configuration appears during later inference, the model does not create a new second-level pattern state for it. Instead, it tries to explain the new configuration using the likelihoods of the second-level states it already learned. The posterior may become spread across several existing states, or the observation may simply fit the model poorly. A new hidden state would require structure learning to be rerun or extended. The same issue applies to paths: if a useful first-level transition never appeared in the training stream, it will not be available as a second-level path label.
The statistical compression assumption is therefore that the coarse states and transitions seen during training are enough for the later task. This assumption may be reasonable in restricted domains. It may also be exactly where the computational savings come from: the model plans only with a smaller set of learned coarse states and paths. But it should be stated explicitly. The learned hierarchy does not guarantee that every reachable, useful, or task-relevant first-level possibility has been represented. This suggests that fast structure learning should be extended to work at test time, enabling continual learning of the hierarchy.

title: Limitations of Renormalizing Generative Models as Hierarchical Planning Models
text:
Preference Lifting
Fast structure learning does not automatically specify how preferences should be used at higher levels of the hierarchy. In standard active-inference planning, preferences are usually defined over observations. For example, if the preferred observation distribution is \(p^*(o)\), then a first-level path \(u^{(1)}\) can be scored through the utility term in the expected free-energy
\[
-\mathbb E_{q(o\mid u^{(1)})}
[
\log p^*(o)
].
\]
This does not require a separate preference distribution over first-level states. The first-level model predicts observations under each candidate path and compares those predicted observations directly with \(p^*(o)\).
The issue appears when planning is moved up one level. A second-level planner does not directly choose among predicted observations. It chooses among second-level paths and predicts second-level states. These second-level states generate or predict first-level states. Therefore, to evaluate second-level plans, the model needs a way to say which first-level states are valuable.
One way to construct this value is to use the first-level likelihood. A first-level state \(s^{(1)}\) can be assigned a value by averaging the original observation preference over the observations it predicts:
\[
V(s^{(1)})
=
\sum_o
P(o\mid s^{(1)})
\log p^*(o).
\]
This induces a preference over first-level states:
\[
p^*(s^{(1)})
\propto
\exp V(s^{(1)}).
\]
A second-level state \(s^{(2)}\) can then be scored through the first-level states it predicts. If the second-level state predicts first-level states through \(P(s^{(1)}\mid s^{(2)})\), its value can be written as
\[
V(s^{(2)})
=
\sum_{s^{(1)}}
P(s^{(1)}\mid s^{(2)})
\log p^*(s^{(1)}).
\]
This is the preference-lifting step. It converts preferences over observations into preferences over first-level states, so that second-level planning can evaluate abstract states and paths.
The caveat is that this only works well if the abstraction preserves value-relevant distinctions. Suppose two first-level states, \(s_a^{(1)}\) and \(s_b^{(1)}\), are both generated by the same second-level state \(s^{(2)}\). If \(s_a^{(1)}\) tends to generate preferred observations but \(s_b^{(1)}\) tends to generate dispreferred observations, then the value of \(s^{(2)}\) averages over an important difference. The high-level planner may no longer know whether moving toward \(s^{(2)}\) is good or bad.
Thus preference lifting is not merely a notational issue. A higher-level state can be assigned a value through the lower-level states and observations it predicts, but this value is useful for planning only if the higher-level abstraction has not merged lower-level states that should remain separate for the task. This suggests one should perhaps incorporate value in the way states are lumped together in future work.
This is a real gap, but the required object is clear: a decoder or value map from higher-level states to the lower-level variables on which preferences are defined. The deeper problem is whether the learned higher-level paths have valid control semantics, as we’ll see next.

title: Limitations of Renormalizing Generative Models as Hierarchical Planning Models
section: Learned Paths Are Not Automatically Actions
text:
Learned Paths Are Not Automatically Actions
In an RGM, a path value selects one transition rule:
\[
P(s_{t+1}\mid s_t,u_t).
\]
At the second level, this means that a learned path label \(u^{(2)}\) selects a transition among second-level states. If a path is marked as controllable, the reference planning routine can score that path using expected free energy. In that case, the agent can choose among path values.
The issue is that fast structure learning does not learn which transitions are interventions. It learns which transitions were observed in the training stream. A learned path \(u^{(2)}\) therefore means “this second-level transition occurred,” not necessarily “the agent can choose this second-level transition.”
This is enough for prediction, but not for action.
The problem appears when an observed transition combines controllable and uncontrollable changes. If the whole transition is treated as a selectable high-level path, the planner may treat an exogenous change as if it were under the agent’s control.
For example, suppose a second-level state labels a first-level configuration with two components:
\[
s_{\mathrm{loc}}^{(1)}
=
(r,h),
\]
where \(r\) is the weather state and \(h\) is the umbrella state. Rain is exogenous, while the umbrella state is controllable. Suppose the training stream contains the coarse transition
\[
(\text{rain},\text{open})
\to
(\text{dry},\text{closed}).
\]
Fast structure learning can assign this transition a path label \(u^{(2)}\). As a prediction, this is fine: this transition occurred in the data. But as an action, it is wrong. Selecting this path would mean selecting both that the umbrella closes and that the rain stops.
A valid controllable option should only control the umbrella, for example
\[
\beta^{(2)}
=
\text{close umbrella}.
\]
The weather dynamics should remain exogenous:
\[
P(r',h'\mid r,h,\beta^{(2)})
=
P(r'\mid r)
P(h'\mid r,h,\beta^{(2)}),
\]
where \(r\) denotes the weather state and \(h\) denotes the umbrella state. The controllable option \(\beta^{(2)}\) can influence \(h'\), but it should not directly select \(r'\).
Thus the main limitation of the current RGM is:
\[
\text{learned path label } u^{(2)}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{controllable option } \beta^{(2)}.
\]
A further classification step is required. Each learned path must be interpreted as either a controllable option, an exogenous transition mode, or a mixed statistical transition that should not be selected as a single action. Fast structure learning does not provide this classification by itself. In future work, fast structure learning could be adapted to not bundle controllable and uncontrollable states together.

title: Limitations of Renormalizing Generative Models as Hierarchical Planning Models
text:
Controllable and Uncontrollable Factors
One possible response is to keep controllable and uncontrollable factors separate during structure learning. For example, the model could learn one second-level factor for controllable state and another for uncontrollable context:
\[
s_{\mathrm{ctrl}}^{(2)}
=
\text{controllable state},
\qquad
s_{\mathrm{ctx}}^{(2)}
=
\text{uncontrollable context}.
\]
Paths of \(s_{\mathrm{ctrl}}^{(2)}\) could then be treated as possible controllable options, while paths of \(s_{\mathrm{ctx}}^{(2)}\) would be inferred as exogenous context. This helps avoid treating a mixed context-control transition as a single action. However, this separation does not solve the whole problem.
The first issue is value dependence. Suppose the observation is
\[
o \in \{\text{dry},\text{wet}\},
\]
and \(\text{wet}\) is strongly unpreferred. Let the relevant hidden state have two components,
\[
(r,h),
\]
where \(r\) is the weather state and \(h\) is the umbrella state. The observation \(\text{wet}\) depends on these variables jointly. For example,
\[
P(o=\text{wet}\mid r=\text{rain},h=\text{closed}) \approx 1,
\]
but
\[
P(o=\text{wet}\mid r=\text{rain},h=\text{open}) \approx 0,
\]
and
\[
P(o=\text{wet}\mid r=\text{dry},h=\text{closed}) \approx 0.
\]
Thus the bad outcome is not caused by rain alone or by a closed umbrella alone. It is caused by their combination.
This matters for preference lifting. If preferences are lifted to the joint state \((r,h)\), there is no problem: the joint state \((\text{rain},\text{closed})\) receives low value, while \((\text{rain},\text{open})\) and \((\text{dry},\text{closed})\) do not. But if preference lifting produces separate preferences over \(r\) and \(h\) by marginalizing out the other variable, then information is lost. The model is forced to assign a value to rain without knowing whether the umbrella is open, and a value to the umbrella state without knowing whether it is raining.
In other words, the true value has the form
\[
V(r,h),
\]
but a separated preference representation approximates it by something like
\[
V_r(r) + V_h(h).
\]
This approximation cannot exactly represent the fact that only the combination \((\text{rain},\text{closed})\) is bad. Therefore, separating controllable and uncontrollable factors can make preference lifting approximate whenever preferences depend on their joint consequences for observations. This suggests that preference lifting should not use this sort of (mean-field) approximation, marginalizing across factors.
The second issue is transition dependence. Suppose the controllable state is location, with values \(\text{outside}\) and \(\text{inside}\), and the contextual state is door status, with values \(\text{locked}\) and \(\text{unlocked}\). The option
\[
\beta^{(2)}=\text{enter}
\]
changes the location only if the door is unlocked. If the door is locked, the same option fails. The correct transition structure is therefore not
\[
P(s_{\mathrm{ctrl},t+1}^{(2)}
\mid
s_{\mathrm{ctrl},t}^{(2)},
\beta_t^{(2)}),
\]
but
\[
P(s_{\mathrm{ctrl},t+1}^{(2)}
\mid
s_{\mathrm{ctrl},t}^{(2)},
s_{\mathrm{ctx},t}^{(2)},
\beta_t^{(2)}).
\]
A general POMDP can represent this in two ways. A tabular POMDP can lump location and door status into one joint state. A factored POMDP can keep them separate while allowing the transition of location to depend on door status. In both cases, the model preserves the dependence between the controllable transition and the uncontrollable context.
The standard RGM construction does not naturally provide this second option. Its factorization does not introduce arbitrary conditional dependencies between factors at the same level. If the transition from outside to inside depends on whether the door is locked, the straightforward RGM representation is therefore to combine location and door status into a single joint factor. This suggests the need for factored RGMs that keep track of conditional dependencies across factors.
But this creates a tension. If location and door status are lumped together, then the model has preserved the context dependence, but it has no longer cleanly separated controllable state from uncontrollable context. If they are separated, then the model can distinguish what is controllable from what is contextual, but it risks losing the conditional transition structure that makes the action model correct.
This is why separating controllable and uncontrollable factors is not sufficient. It prevents one error, namely treating exogenous changes as actions. But it does not guarantee that the model learns how exogenous context changes the effects of controllable actions. Fast structure learning learns empirical states and empirical transition labels from passive data. It does not by itself learn the causal or conditional control structure needed to say that the option \(\text{enter}\) succeeds when the door is unlocked and fails when the door is locked.
Thus the repair is not simply to group only controllable factors together. The stronger requirement is to preserve the dependency scope needed for control. The model must represent what the agent can choose, what it must condition on, and how contextual variables change both the value and the consequences of controllable options.

title: Limitations of Renormalizing Generative Models as Hierarchical Planning Models
text:
Conclusion
Fast structure learning constructs an abstract predictive hierarchy. This hierarchy can support prediction, hierarchical inference, and empirical priors across scales. It should not automatically be interpreted as an abstract control hierarchy.
The computational motivation for hierarchical planning is that a high-level transition can stand for a lower-level episode. A flat planner over horizon \(H^{(2)}H^{(1)}\) faces a primitive policy space on the order of
\[
|\mathcal U^{(1)}|^{H^{(2)}H^{(1)}}.
\]
An ideal two-level planner would replace this with a cost closer to
\[
|\mathcal U^{(2)}|^{H^{(2)}}
+
H^{(2)}|\mathcal U^{(1)}|^{H^{(1)}}.
\]
This reduction is meaningful only if the high-level action space is much smaller than the space of lower-level policy fragments:
\[
|\mathcal U^{(2)}|
\ll
|\mathcal U^{(1)}|^{H^{(1)}}.
\]
Fast structure learning can produce a small empirical set of second-level path labels,
\[
\mathcal P_{\mathrm{FSL}}^{(2)}
\subseteq
(\mathcal U^{(1)})^{H^{(1)}}.
\]
However, a small empirical path set is not necessarily a valid option set. The computational savings are justified only if the learned paths are representative, task-relevant, correctly separated into controllable and exogenous modes, and supplied with lower-level implementations when treated as controllable options.
The main limitations are therefore:

The compression is statistical and depends on the representativeness of the training stream.
Low-level preferences must be lifted through a suitable decoder or value map.
Preference lifting can become approximate if value depends on combinations of factors but preferences are represented separately over those factors.
Learned path labels \(u^{(2)}\) must be classified as controllable options \(\beta^{(2)}\), exogenous transition modes, or mixed statistical transitions.
Contextual variables may need to modulate the value and consequences of controllable options.

The concise conclusion is:
\[
\text{fewer learned paths}
\neq
\text{valid planning abstraction}.
\]
Equivalently, RGMs learn an abstract predictive hierarchy, whereas hierarchical planning requires an abstract control hierarchy.
This distinction preserves the value of the RGM construction while clarifying its current limitation. RGMs build hierarchical models of observed structure. Additional mechanisms, such as those mentioned in this post, are required before the learned hierarchy can be treated as a hierarchy of valid actions.

title: Opportunities
text:
Open projects

Principled hierarchies
Universal world modeling
How should agents learn abstract, hierarchical models of their world? This project connects hierarchical reinforcement learning, causal models, multiscale physics and hierarchical active inference, in theory and in practice.


Who we’re looking for and how to apply

We are looking for: a student with a strong theoretical background and an interest in machine learning; relevant experience is a plus. Ideally full-time or close to it. You would work with a full-time PhD student on the project and experts across ATOM, and lead a paper as first or joint first author, targeting submission by May 2027.
Apply: Email Aman Pawar, cc’ing Lancelot Da Costa, Manoosh Samiei, Ali Gholamzadeh and Andrew Pashea, with the subject “[Principled hierarchies] Your name”, your CV and one or two paragraphs on why you are interested, which areas interest you most, how many hours per week you can commit, and anything not obvious from your CV.



Natural building blocks in practice
Universal world modeling
Develop learnable world-model building blocks that work on their own and combine into hierarchical active inference agents.


Who we’re looking for and how to apply

We are looking for: up to two contributors, one leaning towards modeling and learning, the other towards benchmarking and implementation, with strong Python and a working knowledge of probabilistic models; relevant experience is a plus. Ideally full-time or close to it. The goal is a manuscript and open-source code by May 2027.
Apply: Email Andrew Pashea, cc’ing Lancelot Da Costa, with the subject “[Natural building blocks] Your name”, your CV and a few paragraphs on why you are interested, which strand you lean towards, and how many hours per week you can commit.



LLM-driven structure learning
Model discovery
Use large language models to propose and refine the structure of world models for active inference agents, keeping an interpretable trace of every change. An existing pipeline shows promising first results, and many scientific questions remain open.


Who we’re looking for and how to apply

We are looking for: a motivated student or a team of two to take the project forward, with solid Python and an interest in LLM-based program and model synthesis; experience with probabilistic modelling or active inference is a plus. Ideally full-time or close to it, although strong relevant experience can make up for fewer hours. The goal is a paper at ICML (deadline expected in late January 2027) or NeurIPS (expected in mid-May 2027).
Apply: Email Lancelot Da Costa, cc’ing Tommaso Salvatori, with the subject “[LLM structure learning] Your name”, your CV, a few lines on why this project interests you, and how many hours per week you can commit.



Benchmarking ATOM agents
Evaluation
What are agents that learn like we do good at, and how should we measure it? Review existing reinforcement learning and world modeling benchmarks, learn about how children learn, and design new evaluations.


Who we’re looking for and how to apply

We are looking for: a student interested in reinforcement learning, world modeling and evaluation, and ideally in how children learn; relevant experience is a plus. Ideally full-time or close to it. The goal is a paper at ICML (deadline expected in late January 2027) or NeurIPS (expected in mid-May 2027).
Apply: Email Lancelot Da Costa with the subject “[Benchmarking ATOM agents] Your name”, your CV, a few lines on why this project interests you, and how many hours per week you can commit.
